name: Home-based private school (file a Private School Affidavit)
description: The parent establishes a private school in the home and files the annual Private School Affidavit (PSA, also called the R-4) with the California Department of Education. Children enrolled in a full-time private day school are exempt from public school compulsory attendance under Ed Code 48222. CDE lists the home-based private school as one of the ways to educate a child at home. Filing is a registration, not a license or approval: CDE does not verify the information or evaluate curriculum.
requirements: File the Private School Affidavit online with CDE every school year (statutory filing period October 1-15; CDE's online system is open roughly August 1 through June 30 so new and mid-year schools can file when they start). If you file early in August/September you do not need to file again in October.
Offer instruction in English in the several branches of study required to be taught in the public schools (Ed Code 48222; see Ed Code 51210 and 51220 for grades 1-6 and 7-12 areas of study).
Instruction must be by persons capable of teaching (Ed Code 48222); no teaching credential is required for the parent.
Keep an attendance register that clearly indicates every absence of a half day or more (Ed Code 48222).
Keep current and available at the school: the courses of study offered, and the names and addresses of faculty with a record of each one's educational qualifications (Ed Code 33190).
Students must be ages 6-18 within compulsory education range; the school selects and provides all curricular and instructional materials (CDE).
Criminal record summary requirement of Ed Code 44237 does not apply to a parent working exclusively with his or her own children.
pros: Maximum freedom over curriculum, schedule, worldview (including religious materials) and teaching methods.
No reporting to the school district and no state testing or Physical Fitness Test requirement.
Immunization requirements of H&S Code 120335 do not apply to pupils in a home-based private school.
Parent issues own transcripts, diploma and (as principal) can generally issue work permits to students other than their own children (CDE work permit FAQ).
cons: No public funding; family pays all curriculum, classes and testing costs.
Parent carries full record-keeping and high school transcript/diploma responsibility; some colleges, employers and the military scrutinize home-issued diplomas more closely.
Not eligible for public-school-only programs (e.g., California State Parks Free Fourth Grade Pass, CCAP dual enrollment partnerships, state testing).
Filing information (school name, address of record) is submitted under penalty of perjury and schools with six or more students appear in public CDE data.
legal_basis: Ed Code 33190 (affidavit and records), 48222 (private full-time day school exemption), 44237 (criminal record summary, parent exemption), H&S Code 120335(f) (immunization exemption)

name: Private School Satellite Program (PSP)
description: The family enrolls the child in an existing private school that operates an independent study / home-study program. The PSP (not the family) files the Private School Affidavit and is legally the child's school; the parent teaches at home under the PSP's policies. CDE describes this option as enrolling 'through an existing private school that offers online learning or independent study options.' PSPs range from record-keeping-only services to full-service programs with classes, counseling, transcripts and accreditation.
requirements: Enroll with a PSP that has filed a current Private School Affidavit with CDE (verify the PSP appears in the CDE private school data or ask for a copy of its filing).
Complete the PSP's enrollment forms, statement of intent, and records release/transfer request.
Submit whatever attendance, course lists, grades or work logs the PSP requires so it can maintain the Ed Code 33190 / 48222 records.
Pay any enrollment or service fees set by the PSP (fees vary widely; some are low-cost).
pros: PSP files the PSA and maintains official cumulative records, so family paperwork is lighter.
Transcripts and diplomas are issued by an established private school; some PSPs are accredited (e.g., WASC) which can help with college admissions.
Same curriculum freedom as a home-based private school, including religious materials.
Often provides community: field trips, classes, graduation ceremonies, counselor support.
cons: Costs money (tuition/fees) and no public funds for curriculum.
Must follow the PSP's own rules (reporting deadlines, required subjects, statement of faith for some).
Quality and accreditation vary; families must vet the PSP themselves.
Not eligible for public-school-only programs.
legal_basis: Ed Code 33190 and 48222 (the PSP is the private school that files and keeps records)

name: Public charter school independent study (homeschool charter)
description: The child enrolls in a nonclassroom-based public charter school and completes coursework at home under independent study, supervised by a credentialed teacher of record (often called an Educational Specialist or Supervising Teacher). The student is a public school student. Many homeschool charters provide per-student 'instructional funds' that the school spends (through approved vendors) on curriculum, classes and materials for the family.
requirements: Enroll in a charter school authorized to offer nonclassroom-based independent study (Ed Code 47600 et seq.; independent study under Ed Code 51745-51749.6 and 47612.5).

Sign a written independent study master agreement before instruction begins (Ed Code 51747) covering objectives, methods, assignment frequency, evaluation, duration, and the right to return to classroom instruction.

Meet regularly with the credentialed supervising teacher; provide work samples/learning records each learning period so the school can document attendance through student work product (Ed Code 51747, 5 CCR 11700 et seq.).
Participate in required state testing (CAASPP/ELPAC as applicable) and the Physical Fitness Test in tested grades (Ed Code 60640, 60800).
Use only secular, standards-aligned materials when purchased with public funds; charter schools must be nonsectarian (Ed Code 47605).
Charter cannot give the family funds or any other thing of value directly for independent study (Ed Code 51747.3); purchases are made by the school.
pros: Public funding: no tuition, and many charters provide instructional funds for curriculum, enrichment classes, lessons and supplies.
Credentialed teacher support, special education services and IEPs, counseling, and an accredited public school transcript/diploma (A-G courses at many).
Students are public school students and qualify for public-school programs (e.g., California State Parks Free Fourth Grade Pass, CCAP dual enrollment partnerships).
Immunization requirements do not apply to independent study pupils who receive no classroom-based instruction (H&S 120335(f)).
cons: Must follow state standards, testing, and the charter's reporting/work-sample requirements; less autonomy.
Public funds cannot buy religious curriculum (constitutional challenge Woolard v. Thurmond was pending at the U.S. Supreme Court on cert in late 2026).
Funding amounts, vendor lists and policies differ by charter and can change with state budget or charter renewal.
Families receiving public funds are ineligible for some private homeschool grants (e.g., HSLDA Curriculum Grant).
legal_basis: Ed Code 47600 et seq. (Charter Schools Act), 47612.5, 47634.2 (nonclassroom-based funding determinations), 51745-51749.6 (independent study), 51747.3; 5 CCR 11700-11704

name: Private tutor holding a valid California teaching credential
description: A child may be exempted from public school attendance if instructed by a private tutor (which can be the parent) who holds a valid California teaching credential for the grade level taught. No affidavit filing is required for this option when the Ed Code 48224 conditions are met.
requirements: Tutor holds a valid California state credential for the grade level taught (Ed Code 48224).
Instruction in the several branches of study required in public schools, in English.
At least 3 hours a day for 175 days each calendar year, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. (Ed Code 48224).
Keep attendance records; keep a copy of the credential on file.
pros: No Private School Affidavit filing required.
Full curriculum freedom; useful for credentialed-teacher parents.
Simple legal footing that is well established in statute.
cons: Requires a current California teaching credential appropriate to each child's grade level (most parents do not hold one).
Statutory minimum hours/days and the 8 a.m.-4 p.m. window are less flexible.
Hiring an outside credentialed tutor full-time is expensive.
No public funding; tutor is not a school so diplomas/transcripts need separate planning.

name: Public school district independent study
description: The child stays enrolled in the local school district (or county office of education) and completes work at home through the district's independent study program, under a credentialed supervising teacher. Since 2021-22, every school district and county office of education must offer independent study (with limited exceptions). Short-term and long-term independent study are available; the district provides curriculum.
requirements: Enroll in (or remain in) the district and request placement in its independent study program.
Sign a written independent study agreement before instruction begins (Ed Code 51747), including the student's right to return to in-person instruction.
Complete assignments and submit work product; participate in required synchronous instruction / live interaction as set out in Ed Code 51747 (requirements vary by grade span).
Participate in state testing (CAASPP, ELPAC, Physical Fitness Test in tested grades).
Use district-provided or district-approved curriculum.
pros: Free; curriculum, textbooks and often devices provided.
Stays in the public system: district diploma, IEP/504 services, access to some campus activities and programs.
Easy to return to the classroom; good for short-term or transitional homeschooling.
Eligible for public-school-only programs and CCAP dual enrollment partnerships.
cons: Least curriculum freedom; must follow district materials, pacing and standards.
Regular teacher check-ins, live instruction and testing requirements.
Program quality and flexibility vary greatly by district.
Usually no discretionary 'instructional funds' like those offered by many homeschool charters.
legal_basis: Ed Code 51745-51749.6 (independent study, as amended by AB 130 (2021) and later budget trailer bills); 5 CCR 11700 et seq.
